Admin., 656 F.3d 580 (7th Cir. 2011) (overturning a requirement for electronic 
on-board recorders on certain commercial vehicles because of agency failure to

Sometimes courts blur the distinctions between review of agency 
comphance with its procedural obligations, arbitrary and capricious review 
under the APA, and interpretation of the relevant provisions in substantive 
agency statutes. For example, the D.C. Circuit considered the SEC’s unique 
statutory obligation to consider the effect of a new rule upon “efficiency, 
competition, and capital formation,” 15 U.S.C. §§ 78c(f), 78w(a)(2), 80a-2(c); 
the agency’s failure to consider and make pubhc the economic consequences of 
a proposed regulation made promulgation of the rule arbitrary and capricious 
and not in accordance with law. In Chamber of Commerce v. SEC, 412 F.3d 
133, 144 (D.C. Cir. 2005), the court ruled that the SEC “violated its obligation 
under 15 U.S.C. § 80a—2(c), and therefore the APA, in failing adequately to 
consider the costs imposed” by the two challenged conditions regulating the 
authority of mutual funds to engage in certain transactions. The court :^sed 
the arbitrary and capricious test with the legal requirement of adherence to 
the SEC’s organic statute, holding that the rule was arbitrary and capricious 
because it violated the statute’s analytical requirements. Plainly^ a great deal 
turns on precisely how the substantive provisions of the statute are 
interpreted, an issue we will take up in detail in Chapter 7. For a critique of 
the D.C. Circuit’s approach to review of SEC cost-benefit analyses, see Bruce 
Kraus & Connor Paso, Rational Boundaries for SEC Cost-Benefit-Analysis, 30 
Ya l e J. o n  Re g . 289 (2013).

Remand Without Vacatur. Tn Evaluating Remand without Vacatur: A 
New Judicial Remedy for Defective Agency Rulemakings, 80 N.Y.U. L. Re v . 
278, 278—81 (2005), Kristina Daugirdas describes judicial remand of rules to 
agencies without vacating them:
Until recently, when reviewing courts deemed rules 
promulgated by administrative agencies to be arbitrary and 
capricious, the courts generally vacated the rules before remanding 
them back to the agencies. The consequences of vacating agency 
rules, and thus voiding all or part of a regulatory framework, can be 
severe, particularly in the context of health and safety regulations. 
For example, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration 
estimates that had the D.C. Circuit not vacated a rule requiring 
passive restraints in automobiles, “thousands of fives [would have 
been saved] and millions of serious injuries would have been 
prevented between 1972 and [1987].” * * *
Once a court vacates a rule, the agency may either reenact the 
same rule with an amended justification or replace the old rule with 
a new one that is substantively different; the agency also may
